Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.text: So, sign language names aren't just an arbitrary translation of your spoken name. They're more like a monosyllabic nickname, something short and easy to sign. People usually come up with them, or friends give them to you. They're based on your character traits, your physical appearance, or a nickname you're commonly known by. So a person who's very tall might get the sign for tall. Or there's someone who's very fast, he gets the sign for fast. It's just a sign that you're recognizable by. And some people are more comfortable with having a sign language name that's not based on their actual name. There's also a thing called a borrowed name, which is a sign that's used as your name, but it's not actually your name. But a lot of people will just borrow the sign for their spoken name if the letters of the spoken name have an initial-finger spelling.

Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.text: It's very different from any other language. In sign language, sign names are not a name per se, rather they are a word meaning name. So it's more like calling somebody by their profession or their characteristic or an attribute or a nickname, which is very common in American culture. It's not that different to how we use nicknames in English, and it's actually the same in most cultures. For example, my sign name is "big hand". I have big hands, but it's not my name, but it's a word that describes me. And then people use that word as my name. My sign name, as it's called in sign language, is really my nickname, and I think it's the same in most cultures.

items.text: It works the same as regular spoken names, as in, if a name is not easily pronounced, it gets shortened. So the name is not an exact spelling of the name, it's an approximation. So like "Johanna" becomes J-A, "Daphne" becomes D-P, and so on. It's just a visual representation of the name, so you're just going to use the letters. But then it's very different in that it has to be something that works as a symbol, so like a shape that is memorable. So for me, my name is P-C. But it's a weird shape, a loop and a curve. And that's the name.

items.text:
Hi,

You ask me who the USA is in debt to. The US national debt is about $31 trillion, so the answer is not simply one or two parties. Roughly 16% of the US debt is held by the public, meaning investors, institutions, and other foreign governments. The rest is held by the government itself.

The US government has been borrowing money for years. They have borrowed money from other countries too, with the largest holder of US debt being Japan, which holds about 11% of the debt. This is a good example of the debt being spread out. The debt is not simply owed to one or two people.

I hope this answers your question.

Kind regards,

John

items.text:
Hi Tom,
thanks for your question. I think you mean how does a mammal stay hydrated in the ocean.
I think I remember something about whales can use sea water to hydrate their cells, so the sea water has salt in it, and it has the same level of salt as our blood cells, so they can just take in the water, and it's like putting saline into our blood cells, it's exactly the same salt concentration. But then they also have the mechanism to be able to expel the excess salt. So it's a two-part system. They can take in sea water and hydrate. But they also have to be able to expel the salt, and they do that through their kidneys. They're really good at it, they are really good at it. But there are some saltwater mammals that can't take in the salt water. So they have to go out of the water to get some fresh water. So for a whale, it's not a big deal. But for a manatee, which is a saltwater mammal, it has to go on land, to get fresh water. So it's a very interesting system.
So the short answer to your question is, it's a very interesting system. Some can stay in the water, some can't. But all of them, they have to expel the salt, they have to pee out the salt.
Cheers
Nick

So the kidneys in marine mammals are very specialized. So if you look at a seal, for example, it has very, very small kidneys. And these small kidneys are quite specialized and can excrete salt. So it can hydrate itself through drinking salt water. The kidneys will remove the salt and excrete it. And that's how the marine mammals can hydrate themselves.
That's why it's called the salt excretion.

Question: why child support is based on income rather than what a child would need monthly.
items.text: The point of child support guidelines is not to exactly calculate what a child needs each month. Its purpose is to approximate the share of income that would have been available for the child if the parents were living together, so that a child is not worse off because of a divorce. So, if dad makes $100,000 and mom makes $50,000, guidelines would say that if they were together, $150,000 would be available for the child. That is why the guidelines look at gross income. There's a lot of stuff that can be modified. It's a starting point, not a strict rule. But, if the child needs more, there's the concept of deviation from guidelines. I see a lot of cases where the court will deviate from guidelines in the child's interest. In fact, I think in most states, the court has the authority to deviate from the guidelines.

But the law doesn't want to spend resources on individualized needs of each kid, which is very difficult to calculate. But if you have other parents who have higher income than you, you can get more. But as a default, it's based on the income of the parents.

Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.text: Watching popcorn pop is one of those things that seems like it should be just a toy for kids, but I'm quite convinced we're missing some very simple physics. And what's actually happening inside the kernel is like a pressure cooker with a tiny explosive. The corn kernel is a very hard shell, which is full of hard starch and moisture. The moisture is the key. The moisture is what will turn into steam and build up the pressure and turn into steam. So you'll get the steam pressure to a point where it can't be contained anymore, and it explodes. So the steam is pushing on the starch and the starch, which is inside the shell, is being pushed and stretched into a foam-like structure. And at some point, the shell breaks. So, when I eat popcorn, I'm eating a very thin foam-like starch, which is being held together by a thin shell. And I think we're missing out by not understanding how the moisture is the driving force of the whole thing. The moisture is what's making the pressure. Without the moisture, you can't get the steam. You can't get the foam. Without the foam, you get a hard kernel. So I think we're missing something very important, and I think we're missing it because popcorn is just a toy, and the fact that it's a toy doesn't mean that you shouldn't study its physics. And I think if we could figure out the right amount of moisture, we could make a better product. That's what's driving it.

Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.text:
I think most people assume that popcorn popping is primarily a water story, and while water vapor pressure is indeed the ultimate cause of the rupture, I think we underplay the role of the kernel's structure. I want to draw attention to the fact that the hard shell is the main event. That shell is a hardened structure of polysaccharides and lignin, and it's a pressure vessel. The kernel will have water inside in a liquid state, and the water vapor pressure builds up and the hard shell is the pressure vessel. But there is also a starch matrix inside that's gelatinizing. And then, at some point the shell can no longer contain the pressure, it fails, and the water vaporizes and the starch matrix, being now hot, expands. And then the starch cools and forms an amorphous solid. So, when we see this puffed thing that is popcorn, it's actually the starch that is the bulk of what we see.

And I think this is the main point. We think of popcorn as being a water event, a water vapor event, but it's not really a water event. The shell fails, the water expands the matrix, and it's all about the starch. We eat popcorn. We don't eat water. What we eat is starch that's been expanded and then cooled down into a solid structure. And it's a very interesting structure, very interesting, because it's amorphous, it's not a crystal, it's not crystalline, it's an amorphous solid. So it's a solid, but it's a glass, and the starch has transformed into a glass. So, I think it's interesting to think about what we actually eat. We eat a solidified glass structure of starch.

And so I think what happens is, we've got pressure building up, and the shell fails and the water vaporizes and the starch matrix expands. And then it cools down and becomes a solid. But it's a solid, not a liquid, not a gas, it's a solid. But it's not a crystal, it's a glass. So it's interesting to think about how glass is an amorphous solid. Glass is not a crystal, it's an amorphous solid. And the popcorn, that's the actual food that we eat.

items.text:
I think we take it for granted. We sit around, grab the bag, and hear the crackle, but I think the true drama is happening entirely within the kernel. I remember my grandmother's kitchen, and I have tried to understand the science that's happening inside the kernel. And it's pretty dramatic. Each kernel has a hard shell, and inside there's a tiny bit of water, plus the starchy endosperm. The water is under pressure when you put it on the stove. The shell prevents it from boiling off, so the pressure builds, the temperature climbs. Then, it pops. And the pressure inside the kernel is high enough that it breaks the shell. So, the pressure drops, the water instantly flashes into steam. It expands about 40 times in volume. And the starchy endosperm, which is like paste, becomes puffy white foam. That's the popcorn.
But I don't like popcorn. I like the smell, the crackle. But I don't like the popcorn itself. The kernel has to be a certain size. And you have to heat it slowly. And then, when you heat it, it'll pop. And you can tell, if you know how to look at the kernel, how big the pop will be. So, that's why I think people buy bagged popcorn in stores. But the corn is smaller. I think the big kernels are better, and you can tell just by looking at them. The big ones will pop big. The small ones will pop small. The kernel will expand, and the steam will push the starchy endosperm out. And it becomes puffy white foam. And that's popcorn.

Question: Why is the history of math so separated from math itself in education? Wouldn't it be more interesting if this weren't the case?
items.text:
Hi

Great question. I feel you. The way we teach math is extremely dry, no context for what we're doing. History is a good way to show how a subject emerged and developed.

One reason I think the two are separated is that we like math to be presented as timeless truths. Like 2+2=4 has always been true. That's true but it's not how we understand that fact. We didn't jump from the Stone Age to modern math. We developed it in stages. The problem with history is that we can't really teach kids every stage of development. The history of math is very long and complex. There's too much to pack into a school curriculum.

Yes I think it would be more engaging if we wove in history. But I think what we need is to show students the context of what we're doing. Not necessarily the history itself, but why we do it.

Love
Mark

Question: Why does metal react so violently when microwaved?
items.text: The effect is caused by the interaction of microwaves with metal particles. In a microwave, the waves induce electrical currents on the surface of a metal object. These currents get trapped on the metal. When the currents become large, the metal heats up. This can produce a spark or arc between the metal and the oven wall. The arc will heat up the air inside the oven, and it will produce a ball of plasma. Plasma is hot, but it's also a very good conductor of electricity. The plasma ball is a good conductor because it contains ions and free electrons. It's very hot, and it's very conductive. The plasma ball is very conductive, and it will expand, it will get bigger. That's what you see.

A simple rain gauge measures rainfall by catching precipitation in a funnel and directing it into a cylindrical measuring tube. 

To ensure accurate and easy reading, the gauge's top opening is deliberately wider than the inner measuring tube. This difference in diameter acts as an amplifier. For example, if the collection opening has ten times the area of the inner tube, one inch of rainfall will fill the tube to a height of ten inches. This magnification allows observers to easily and precisely read very small amounts of rainfall, such as hundredths of an inch.

However, these instruments are subject to errors. One common source of inaccuracy is evaporation; collected water can quickly evaporate before it is measured, especially in warm or windy weather. Another major source is wind exposure. Strong winds can create turbulence around the gauge's mouth, carrying raindrops over the opening and causing the instrument to underestimate the actual rainfall.

items.text:
People often conflate tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, and typhoons. They're not quite the same. So let's clear it up.

A cyclone is the generic term for a low-pressure system with winds rotating around a central core. It can form over land or water. The naming convention for cyclones depends on where they form. In the Pacific, we call it a typhoon. In the Atlantic, it's a hurricane. So the difference between a hurricane and a typhoon is just location. The classification of strength is based on wind speed. A hurricane is defined as having winds over 74 mph. In the Atlantic and Eastern North Pacific. And a typhoon is also defined as having winds over 74 mph. But in the Western North Pacific. So essentially, a hurricane is a cyclone that formed in the Atlantic. A typhoon is a cyclone that formed in the Western North Pacific.

In the Indian Ocean, they're called a cyclone. And in the South Pacific, they're called a cyclone. So the difference between these terms is mostly about geography.

Tornadoes, on the other hand, are completely different. Tornadoes are smaller, more violent, and don't necessarily have to come from a cyclone. They can come out of a storm, or in some cases, can form from a cumulonimbus cloud. Cumulonimbus clouds are the ones that have the mushroom shape. And tornadoes can form over land, and often do. So tornadoes are much smaller than cyclones. Cyclones can be miles and miles across. Tornadoes are often only a few hundred yards across. And they're more violent, but usually much shorter in duration. Whereas cyclones can last days.

A tornado is a funnel cloud or funnel vortex that extends to the ground. Whereas a cyclone, a hurricane, or a typhoon is a big vortex that can be 100 or 200 miles in diameter. And they form over water, typically. And they're very powerful. And they can travel thousands of miles, and can last days. And they're very destructive. But the main difference is the scale. Cyclones are big, tornadoes are small. And tornadoes are more violent. And tornadoes can happen over land, whereas cyclones typically form over water.

Tonight a folded note was tucked between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her floury hands and opened it. *I can't make it to the library before closing. Please keep it another week. I like knowing it's warm.*

Marisol looked at the basket, then at the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing. She wrapped it in wax paper, tucked the note back into the book, and set both by the door. Then she flipped the sign to OPEN and started the coffee.
